claim: Migration of cells in the developing brain is integral for the establishment of neural circuits and function of the central nervous system.
source: Migration of cells in the developing brain is integral for the establishment of neural circuits and function of the central nervous system.
evidence: This is a general statement about the importance of cell migration in brain development, drawing on established scientific knowledge.

claim: Horizontal cells in the zebrafish retina feature several hallmarks of amoeboid-like migration.
source: We found that these cells feature several hallmarks of amoeboid-like migration that enable them to tailor their movements to the spatial constraints of the crowded retina.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observations and data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: Hallmarks of amoeboid-like migration in horizontal cells include cell and nuclear shape changes.
source: These hallmarks include cell and nuclear shape changes, as well as persistent rearward polarization of stable F-actin.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing morphological changes during migration.

claim: Hallmarks of amoeboid-like migration in horizontal cells include persistent rearward polarization of stable F-actin.
source: These hallmarks include cell and nuclear shape changes, as well as persistent rearward polarization of stable F-actin.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data using F-actin markers.

claim: Interference with the organization of the developing retina by changing nuclear properties hampers efficient horizontal cell migration and layer formation.
source: Interference with the organization of the developing retina by changing nuclear properties or overall tissue architecture hampers efficient horizontal cell migration and layer formation showing that cell-tissue interplay is crucial for this process.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from LMNA overexpression experiments.

claim: Interference with the organization of the developing retina by changing overall tissue architecture hampers efficient horizontal cell migration and layer formation.
source: Interference with the organization of the developing retina by changing nuclear properties or overall tissue architecture hampers efficient horizontal cell migration and layer formation showing that cell-tissue interplay is crucial for this process.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from atoh7 morpholino experiments.

claim: Cell-tissue interplay is crucial for horizontal cell migration and layer formation.
source: Interference with the organization of the developing retina by changing nuclear properties or overall tissue architecture hampers efficient horizontal cell migration and layer formation showing that cell-tissue interplay is crucial for this process.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental results showing that tissue-level perturbations affect HC migration.

claim: The amoeboid-like migration mode might be conserved in other areas of the developing nervous system.
source: In view of the high proportion of multipolar migration phenomena observed in brain development, the here uncovered amoeboid-like migration mode might be conserved in other areas of the developing nervous system.
evidence: This is a speculative statement based on the prevalence of multipolar migration in brain development.

claim: Most research on migration mechanisms in the nervous system has focused on radial migration.
source: As of yet however, most research unveiling the cellular and molecular mechanisms of migration in the nervous system has focused on radial migration which entails movements perpendicular to the tissue surface (Angevine and Sidman, 1961; Berry and Rogers, 1965; Morest, 1970b; Morest, 1970a; Rakic, 1971; Walsh and Cepko, 1988; Marin and Rubenstein, 2001; Nadarajah et al., 2001; Nadarajah and Parnavelas, 2002; Cooper, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: During radial migration, neurons determine their direction of movement by establishing process(es) that anchor them to tissue lamina(e) (somal translocation).
source: During radial migration, neurons determine their direction of movement by two different strategies: (1) by establishing process(es) that anchor the migrating neurons to the tissue lamina(e), and thereby facilitating their faithful arrival at their destination (somal translocation) (Nadarajah et al., 2003)
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: During radial migration, neurons determine their direction of movement by moving along radially oriented fibers of radial glia (glia-guided migration).
source: During radial migration, neurons determine their direction of movement by two different strategies: (1) by establishing process(es) that anchor the migrating neurons to the tissue lamina(e), and thereby facilitating their faithful arrival at their destination (somal translocation) (Nadarajah et al., 2003), or (2) by moving along radially oriented fibers of neural progenitors known as radial glia that provide physical scaffolding for migrating neurons (glia-guided migration) (Rakic, 1971; Rakic, 1972; Edmondson and Hatten, 1987; Hatten, 1990; Gertz and Kriegstein, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Neurons displaying multipolar morphology are neither attached to tissue lamina(e) nor move along radial glia fibers.
source: In contrast, neurons that display multipolar morphology are neither attached to the tissue lamina(e) nor move along radial glia fibers.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Multipolar neurons extend multiple dynamic processes in various directions.
source: Instead, these cells were shown to extend multiple dynamic processes in various directions (Tabata and Nakajima, 2003; Honda et al., 2003; Stensaas, 1967; Shoukimas and Hinds, 1978; Gadisseux et al., 1990; Noctor et al., 2004; Nowakowski and Rakic, 1979).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: It is not yet fully understood how multipolar neurons reach their destination with no predisposed migratory information or scaffolds.
source: Despite this prevalence, it is not yet fully understood, how multipolar neurons reach their destination with no predisposed migratory information or scaffolds.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: The zebrafish retina allows for in vivo imaging in a quantitative manner.
source: One central nervous system (CNS) region that allows for in vivo imaging in a quantitative manner is the zebrafish retina (Galli-Resta et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: The mature retina consists of five major neuronal types: photoreceptor, horizontal cell, bipolar cell, amacrine cell, and retinal ganglion cell.
source: The mature retina consists of five major neuronal types: photoreceptor (PR), horizontal cell (HC), bipolar cell (BC), amacrine cell (AC), retinal ganglion cell (RGC), and a single glial cell-type, Müller glia (MG).
evidence: This is established knowledge about retinal cell types.

claim: The mature retina contains a single glial cell-type, Müller glia.
source: The mature retina consists of five major neuronal types: photoreceptor (PR), horizontal cell (HC), bipolar cell (BC), amacrine cell (AC), retinal ganglion cell (RGC), and a single glial cell-type, Müller glia (MG).
evidence: This is established knowledge about retinal cell types.

claim: Retinal neurons reproducibly assemble into three distinct nuclear layers: outer nuclear layer, inner nuclear layer, and ganglion cell layer.
source: During development, retinal neurons move from their birth-site to their ultimate functioning locations (Figure 1A), and reproducibly assemble into three distinct nuclear layers: outer nuclear layer (ONL), inner nuclear layer (INL), ganglion cell layer (GCL) (Figure 1A').
evidence: This is established knowledge about retinal development and is illustrated in Figure 1A'.

claim: Synapses between retinal layers form at two nuclei-free layers: the outer plexiform layer and the inner plexiform layer.
source: Synapses between these layers form at two nuclei-free layers, known as plexiform layers: the outer plexiform layer (OPL) and the inner plexiform layer (IPL) (Figure 1A').
evidence: This is established knowledge about retinal structure and is illustrated in Figure 1A'.

claim: Division of neuronal progenitors generates committed HC precursors at the apical surface of the retina.
source: Division of neuronal progenitors generates committed HC precursors (HCprs) at the apical surface of the retina.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: HC precursors initially migrate radially from their birth-site to the center of the INL while keeping an attachment to the apical surface and featuring a bipolar morphology.
source: HCprs initially migrate radially from their birth-site to the center of the INL while keeping an attachment to the apical surface and featuring a bipolar morphology (Phase 1).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Upon detachment of their apical anchorage, HC precursors acquire a multipolar morphology.
source: Upon detachment of this anchorage (Figure 1B, Figure 1—figure supplement 1C, Video 2), HCprs acquire a multipolar morphology (Hinds and Hinds, 1979) and migrate with frequent direction changes (Phase 2) (Chow et al., 2015; Amini et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research and illustrated in figures.

claim: HC precursors undergo a terminal division en route to their destination.
source: En route to their destination, HCprs undergo a terminal division (Edqvist and Hallböök, 2004; Weber et al., 2014; Chow et al., 2015; Amini et al., 2019) at diverse depths within the INL giving rise to two postmitotic HCs which migrate toward the HC layer (Godinho et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Migration behavior of HC precursors and postmitotic HCs is similar.
source: We previously showed that migration behavior of HCprs and postmitotic HCs is similar (Amini et al., 2019), which is why we will use the term HC from here on in this manuscript to refer to both.
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research by the authors.

claim: HCs do not move along radially oriented bipolar cells.
source: Thus, we conclude that the radially oriented BCs or MG fibers are unlikely to be prerequisites for HC movement.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing HC migration trajectories relative to BC positions.

claim: HCs do not move along radially oriented Müller glia fibers.
source: Thus, we conclude that the radially oriented BCs or MG fibers are unlikely to be prerequisites for HC movement.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing HC migration trajectories relative to MG positions.

claim: Laminin α1 is only detected in the basement membrane of the retina at all developmental stages.
source: Our results showed that anti-Laminin α1 and HA were only detected in the basement membrane of the retina at all developmental stages (Figure 2A-B, arrowheads) and never within the INL wherein HC migration takes place.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from immunofluorescence staining shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Hyaluronic acid is only detected in the basement membrane of the retina at all developmental stages.
source: Our results showed that anti-Laminin α1 and HA were only detected in the basement membrane of the retina at all developmental stages (Figure 2A-B, arrowheads) and never within the INL wherein HC migration takes place.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from HA biosensor shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Laminin α1 and hyaluronic acid are never detected within the INL wherein HC migration takes place.
source: Our results showed that anti-Laminin α1 and HA were only detected in the basement membrane of the retina at all developmental stages (Figure 2A-B, arrowheads) and never within the INL wherein HC migration takes place.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 2A-B.

claim: It is unlikely that HCs use ECM scaffolds as a main migratory substrate to reach their final destination.
source: Thus, it is unlikely that HCs use ECM scaffolds as a main migratory substrate to reach their final destination.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing lack of ECM components in the INL.

claim: Brillouin shift maps revealed that the lens had higher Brillouin shifts than the retinal neuroepithelium at 48 hpf.
source: These maps revealed that in comparison to the retinal neuroepithelium, the lens had higher Brillouin shifts at 48 hpf (Figure 2D'–E') which further increased as development progressed (70 hpf) (Figure 2D''–E'').
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from Brillouin microscopy shown in Figures 2D'-E'.

claim: Brillouin shifts of the lens further increased as development progressed to 70 hpf.
source: These maps revealed that in comparison to the retinal neuroepithelium, the lens had higher Brillouin shifts at 48 hpf (Figure 2D'–E') which further increased as development progressed (70 hpf) (Figure 2D''–E'').
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from Brillouin microscopy shown in Figures 2D''-E''.

claim: At 70 hpf, the two nuclear-free plexiform layers (OPL and IPL) showed lower Brillouin shifts than the three nuclear layers (ONL, INL, GCL).
source: Notably, Brillouin shift maps of 70 hpf retinae revealed a layered, heterogenous pattern that matched the retinal layers observed in confocal images (Figure 2D''–E''). While the two nuclear-free plexiform layers (OPL and IPL) showed lower Brillouin shifts, the three nuclear layers (ONL, INL, GCL) displayed comparably higher Brillouin shifts.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from Brillouin microscopy shown in Figures 2D''-E''.

claim: Brillouin shift values could be influenced by nuclear occupation.
source: This indicated a correlation between Brillouin shift maps and features of each retinal layer. It further revealed that Brillouin shift values could be influenced by nuclear occupation, as shown previously for fibroblasts (Zhang et al., 2017).
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data and supported by citation to previous research.

claim: Brillouin shift values in the INL showed no obvious differences along the apico-basal axis during and after HC migration.
source: However, Brillouin shift values in the INL showed no obvious differences along the apico-basal axis, during (Figure 2D'–E') and after HC migration (Figure 2D''–E'').
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from Brillouin microscopy shown in Figures 2D'-E'' and 2D''-E''.

claim: HC migration occurs in a homogenous environment without notable local compressibility gradients.
source: Thus, HC migration seems to occur in a homogenous environment without notable local compressibility gradients.
evidence: This is inferred from the Brillouin microscopy data.

claim: No extracellular space between neighboring cells within the INL was detected during periods of HC migration.
source: To this end, we performed live imaging of double-transgenic zebrafish embryos Tg(lhx-1:eGFP) × Tg(βactin:mKate2-ras) labeling HCs and membrane of all retinal cells, respectively. No extracellular space between neighboring cells within the INL was detected during periods of HC migration (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B-B').
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from live imaging shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B-B'.

claim: The developing INL contains closely packed cells but no detectable ECM components during neurogenesis.
source: Thus, similar to the neuroepithelial stage (Matejčić et al., 2018), also during neurogenesis, the developing INL seemed to contain closely packed cells but no detectable ECM components.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and citation to previous research.

claim: HCs migrate through a physically constraining cell-dense tissue with no preexisting path.
source: This suggested that HCs migrate through a physically constraining cell-dense tissue with no preexisting path.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing dense cell packing and lack of ECM.

claim: No tissue ruptures or holes were detected at the peak of HC migration or after HC migration.
source: To test whether ruptures in the tissue existed, which could hint toward protease activities of the migrating cells, tissue integrity was probed using double-transgenic zebrafish retinae Tg(lhx-1:eGFP) × Tg(βactin:mKate2-ras) labeling HCs and PRs, and the membranes of all retinal cells, respectively. We did not detect any tissue ruptures or holes, neither at the peak of HC migration nor after HC migration (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B-B').
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from live imaging shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B-B'.

claim: Protease-dependent path generation might not be a major component in HC migration through the crowded retina.
source: Thus, protease-dependent path generation to move through the crowded retina might not a major component in this context.
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of tissue ruptures observed in the experimental data.

claim: Cell-shape changes in migrating HCs were accompanied by alterations in nuclear perimeter, elongation ratio, and sphericity.
source: These cell-shape changes were accompanied by alterations in nuclear perimeter (μm), elongation ratio, and sphericity (%) (Figure 3A'' and C–E) and dynamic indentations of the nucleus (Figure 3—figure supplement 1E-E', Video 5).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in figures.

claim: In some cases, migrating HCs featured cellular deformations when encountering a neighboring cell that entered mitosis.
source: To test whether a correlation between encountered tissue obstacles and HC shape and direction changes existed, we monitored HC migration (Tg(lhx-1:eGFP)) in relation to the surrounding local environment (Tg(hsp70-H2B:RFP)). We noted that in some cases migrating HCs featured cellular deformations when encountering a neighboring cell that entered mitosis (Figure 3F–I, Video 6).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in figures.

claim: The adaptive cellular and nuclear deformations shown by HCs seemed reversible after circumventing the encountered physical barrier.
source: Notably, the adaptive cellular and nuclear deformations shown by HCs seemed reversible after circumventing the encountered physical barrier (Figure 3F–I, Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in figures.

claim: Migrating HCs tailor their cellular and nuclear shapes, paths and directions to their cell-dense surrounding tissue environment.
source: Together, these data make us speculate that migrating HCs tailor their cellular and nuclear shapes, paths and directions to their cell-dense surrounding tissue environment.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the experimental data.

claim: HCs display membrane blebs during mitosis but never during migration.
source: As seen for many other cell types (Boss, 1955; Burton and Taylor, 1997; Fishkind et al., 1991; Boucrot and Kirchhausen, 2007), HCs displayed membrane blebs during mitosis but never during migration (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A, Video 7).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in figures and citations to previous research.

claim: HCs feature multiple dynamic protrusions with different directionality as they moved within the INL.
source: In contrast, we found that HCs feature multiple dynamic protrusions with different directionality as they moved sideways (tangentially), up (toward the apical), or down (toward the basal) within the INL.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from membrane imaging.

claim: HC protrusions showed different thicknesses, lengths, morphologies (branched vs. unbranched), and orientations.
source: These protrusions showed different thicknesses, lengths, morphologies (branched vs. unbranched), and orientations, and exhibited dynamic extension and retraction from the cell soma in multiple directions (Figure 4A, Video 7).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in figures.

claim: At times, two or multiple protrusions were seen to extend from the cell body at the cell front.
source: At times, two or multiple protrusions were seen to extend from the cell body at the cell front (Figure 4A, Figure 4—figure supplement 1B), another feature also reported for amoeboid migrating cells (Weber et al., 2013; Renkawitz et al., 2019; Kameritsch and Renkawitz, 2020).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in figures and citations to previous research.

claim: The overall probability of finding protrusions with orientations parallel to the direction of cell movement was higher than finding protrusions pointing in other directions.
source: This analysis revealed that the overall probability of finding protrusions with orientations parallel to the direction of cell movement was higher than finding protrusions pointing in other directions (Figure 4C, Figure 4—figure supplement 1F'-I').
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from protrusion tracking shown in figures.

claim: HCs show some front-back polarity while migrating.
source: This implied that HCs show some front-back polarity while migrating.
evidence: This is inferred from the protrusion orientation data.

claim: Lifeact was observed in the cell soma and protrusions of migrating HCs.
source: We found that while Lifeact was observed in the cell soma and protrusions (Figure 4D, Video 9), Utr-CH was absent from the cell soma, membrane-proximal regions, and protrusions (Figure 4E, Video 10).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in figures.

claim: Utrophin was absent from the cell soma, membrane-proximal regions, and protrusions of migrating HCs.
source: We found that while Lifeact was observed in the cell soma and protrusions (Figure 4D, Video 9), Utr-CH was absent from the cell soma, membrane-proximal regions, and protrusions (Figure 4E, Video 10).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in figures.

claim: Utrophin is enriched at the back of the migrating HC.
source: Instead, measurements of Utr-CH fluorescent intensity profiles along the cell axis showed its enrichment at the back of the migrating HC (Figure 4D and F', Figure 4—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in figures.

claim: The uropod-like structure in HCs underwent dynamic changes of extension and retraction.
source: Monitoring Utr-CH during HC migration showed that the uropod-like structure underwent dynamic changes of extension and retraction (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C-D, Video 10), a feature previously reported for amoeboid migrating neutrophils (Manley et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in figures and citation to previous research.

claim: HC centrosomes displayed a highly variable and dynamic localization and continuously shifted their positions from the cell-front to the cell-back while occasionally staying in the cell's middle.
source: Our analysis revealed that HC centrosomes displayed a highly variable and dynamic localization and continuously shifted their positions from the cell-front to the cell-back while occasionally staying in the cell's middle (Figure 4G–H, Figure 4—figure supplement 2B-D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in figures.

claim: Centrosome position did not directly influence the direction of HC movement.
source: This oscillating configuration suggested that centrosome position did not directly influence the direction of HC movement.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data on centrosome dynamics.

claim: HCs acquire a polarized morphology with persistent rearward polarization of stable F-actin, most likely without contribution of centrosome position.
source: Overall, we concluded that similarly to amoeboid moving cells, HCs acquire a polarized morphology with persistent rearward polarization of stable F-actin, most likely without contribution of centrosome position.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data on F-actin distribution and centrosome dynamics.

claim: Increasing the expression of Lamin A (LMNA) at the tissue scale could influence HC migration.
source: Thus, we probed whether and how increasing the expression of Lamin A (LMNA) at the tissue scale could influence HC migration.
evidence: This is the rationale for the experimental approach.

claim: In control heat-shocked retinae, all HCs were positioned within the HC layer at 90 hpf.
source: Similarly, in control heat-shocked retinae, all HCs were positioned within the HC layer at 90 hpf (Figure 5A), showing that heat-shock treatment of the embryos does not impair HC migration and layer formation.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Heat-shock treatment of the embryos does not impair HC migration and layer formation.
source: Similarly, in control heat-shocked retinae, all HCs were positioned within the HC layer at 90 hpf (Figure 5A), showing that heat-shock treatment of the embryos does not impair HC migration and layer formation.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: In LMNA overexpressing retinae, many HCs were found at ectopic basal positions at 90 hpf.
source: In contrast, in the LMNA overexpressing retinae, many HCs were found at ectopic basal positions, mostly within the INL and at times even in the GCL at 90 hpf (Figure 5B, arrowheads).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: While the majority of HCs in LMNA overexpressed conditions reached the HC layer at 92 hpf, a subset of HCs remained at ectopic basal positions.
source: We found that while the majority of HCs in LMNA overexpressed conditions reached the HC layer at 92 hpf, a subset of HCs remained at ectopic basal positions (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: In tissue-scale LMNA overexpressed conditions, many HCs failed to move back toward the apical INL.
source: Analyzing the migration trajectories of tracked HCs revealed that in tissue-scale LMNA overexpressed conditions, many HCs failed to move back toward the apical INL (Figure 5D–E, Figure 5—figure supplement 1B) and consequently resided in ectopic basal positions away from their final position (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in figures.

claim: LMNA overexpressed HCs surrounded by cells not expressing LMNA migrated very similarly to controls and successfully reached the HC layer.
source: LMNA overexpressed HCs surrounded by cells not expressing LMNA migrated very similarly to controls and successfully reached the HC layer (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Mosaic LMNA overexpression of HCs alone does not impede HC migration and layer formation.
source: Thus, while mosaic LMNA overexpression of HCs alone does not impede HC migration and layer formation, changing the nuclear laminar composition at the tissue scale hampers the migration efficiency of HCs causing less efficient HC migration and leading to cells never reaching their final position.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data comparing mosaic and tissue-wide LMNA overexpression.

claim: Changing the nuclear laminar composition at the tissue scale hampers the migration efficiency of HCs causing less efficient HC migration and leading to cells never reaching their final position.
source: Thus, while mosaic LMNA overexpression of HCs alone does not impede HC migration and layer formation, changing the nuclear laminar composition at the tissue scale hampers the migration efficiency of HCs causing less efficient HC migration and leading to cells never reaching their final position.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from tissue-wide LMNA overexpression.

claim: The IPL, once formed, negatively influences the depth of HC migration, as HCs did not basally pass it.
source: We previously showed that the IPL, once formed, negatively influences the depth of HC migration, as HCs did not basally pass it (Amini et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research by the authors.

claim: The IPL may act as a non-passable obstacle for migrating HCs.
source: This suggested that the IPL, despite being devoid of cell bodies, may act as a non-passable obstacle for migrating HCs.
evidence: This is inferred from previous observations.

claim: In atoh7 morphants before emergence of the IPL at 50–55 hpf, the maximal depth of HC migration increased significantly and many HCs were located at the most basal side of the retina adjacent to the basement membrane.
source: Our immunofluorescence stainings of Tg(lhx-1:eGFP) retinae revealed that in atoh7 morphants before emergence of the IPL at 50–55 hpf and, the maximal depth of HC migration increased significantly and that many HCs were located at the most basal side of the retina adjacent to the basement membrane (Figure 6A – bottom panel, red arrowhead, Figure 6C), a depth never seen for HCs in control embryos (Figure 6A – top panel, Figure 6C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A and 6C.

claim: Upon interference with RGC emergence, HCs reached deeper positions in the tissue by moving beyond their typical basal stopping-point.
source: Thus, upon interference with RGC emergence, HCs reached deeper positions in the tissue by moving beyond their typical basal stopping-point.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data in atoh7 morphants.

claim: While all HCs reached the HC layer at 82 hpf in control retinae, many HCs were ectopically located at the most basal retinal layer in atoh7 morphants.
source: We found that while all HCs reached the HC layer at 82 hpf in control retinae (Figure 6B – top panel, Figure 6C), many HCs were ectopically located at the most basal retinal layer in atoh7 morphants (Figure 6B – bottom panel, arrowheads, Figure 6C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6B and 6C.

claim: Before IPL formation, HCs successfully turned back apically from their ectopic basal positions adjacent to the basal membrane and reached the HC layer in atoh7 morphants.
source: We found that before IPL formation, HCs successfully turned back apically from their ectopic basal positions adjacent to the basal membrane (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A – dotted line) and reached the HC layer in atoh7 morphants (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A-B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A-B.

claim: The ability of HCs to move back apically is not lost in the absence of RGCs.
source: This implies that the ability of HCs to move back apically is not lost in the absence of RGCs but that during or after IPL formation, ectopically located HCs failed to pass through the IPL and hence remained trapped in ectopic locations beneath the IPL (Figure 6D–E, Figure 6—figure supplement 1C-D).
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data in atoh7 morphants.

claim: During or after IPL formation, ectopically located HCs failed to pass through the IPL and remained trapped in ectopic locations beneath the IPL.
source: This implies that the ability of HCs to move back apically is not lost in the absence of RGCs but that during or after IPL formation, ectopically located HCs failed to pass through the IPL and hence remained trapped in ectopic locations beneath the IPL (Figure 6D–E, Figure 6—figure supplement 1C-D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in figures.

claim: Ectopically located HCs moved in all directions adjacent to the IPL until they underwent apoptosis.
source: Interestingly, these ectopically located HCs moved in all directions adjacent to the IPL (Figure 6—figure supplement 1C-D), until they underwent apoptosis, evidenced by their progressive fragmentations, immobility, and ultimately disappearance.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1C-D.

claim: The IPL despite being more compressible than the nuclear layers represents a barrier through which migrating HCs are not able to pass when trapped beneath.
source: Overall, we conclude that the IPL despite being more compressible than the nuclear layers (Figure 2D–E'') represents a barrier through which migrating HCs are not able to pass when trapped beneath.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data in atoh7 morphants and Brillouin microscopy.

claim: The IPL likely poses a limit to the morphological adaptability of HCs and their nuclei.
source: Thus, the IPL likely poses a limit to the morphological adaptability of HCs and their nuclei.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing HCs cannot pass through the IPL.

claim: HCs and their precursors follow principles of space adaptation strategies including repeated and reversible shape and direction change to navigate through the complex and densely packed environment of the developing retina.
source: We here showed that HCs and their precursors follow principles of space adaptation strategies including repeated and reversible shape and direction change to navigate through the complex and densely packed environment of the developing retina.
evidence: This is a summary of the experimental findings.

claim: This is the first study describing a cell ultimately becoming a neuron that undergoes amoeboid-like migration in a part of the developing CNS.
source: To the best of our knowledge, this is the first study describing a cell ultimately becoming a neuron that undergoes amoeboid-like migration in a part of the developing CNS.
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the findings.

claim: Changing tissue properties can feedback on the efficiency of amoeboid-like migration and layer formation.
source: We further uncovered that changing tissue properties can feedback on the efficiency of amoeboid-like migration and layer formation, most likely by influencing the space negotiation capability of HCs.
evidence: This is a summary of the experimental findings from LMNA overexpression and atoh7 morpholino experiments.

claim: HCs do not travel along radially oriented progenitors (MGs), or neurons (BCs).
source: As opposed to neocortical neurons including projection neurons which en route to their destination switch from multipolar to bipolar morphology and resume unidirectional radial migration along radial glia fibers (Nadarajah et al., 2003; Nadarajah et al., 2001; Cooper, 2014), HCs do not travel along radially oriented progenitors (MGs), or neurons (BCs).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and citations to previous research.

claim: It is possible that HCs use their neighboring neurons as substrate over which to migrate in all directions (x, y, z) to reach their destination.
source: It is however possible that HCs use their neighboring neurons as substrate over which to migrate in all directions (x, y, z) to reach their destination.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about possible mechanisms.

claim: During long stretches of their migration, HCs follow unconventional tortuous migratory tracks while frequently alternating between radial (up and down) and tangential (lateral) routes.
source: During long stretches of their migration, HCs follow unconventional tortuous migratory tracks while frequently alternating between radial (up and down) and tangential (lateral) routes.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data on HC migration trajectories.

claim: The flexible trajectories and space adaptation strategies allow HCs to move in all dimensions to overcome obstacles within the crowded environment.
source: We hence speculate that the flexible trajectories (Amini et al., 2019) and space adaptation strategies allow HCs to move in all dimensions to overcome obstacles within the crowded environment.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the experimental data.

claim: While HCs reproducibly and robustly reach the HC layer, their path selection is not intrinsically programmed but is rather influenced by the cellular surroundings and the tissue-scale parameters they encounter in their local environment.
source: Thus, while HCs reproducibly and robustly reach the HC layer, their path selection is not intrinsically programmed as opposed to most other retinal neurons (e.g., PRs and RGCs) but is rather influenced by the cellular surroundings and the tissue-scale parameters they encounter in their local environment.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing variable HC trajectories.

claim: The amoeboid-like migration mode exhibited by HCs is not based on bleb formation but correlates with multiple highly dynamic actin-filled protrusions.
source: The amoeboid-like migration mode exhibited by HCs is not based on bleb formation but correlates with multiple highly dynamic actin-filled protrusions.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data on HC protrusions.

claim: HC protrusions are rather involved in probing the tissue environment and pathfinding than directly propelling the movement.
source: Our observation that protrusions are simultaneously extended toward multiple directions, especially during periods in which HCs stay stationary, suggests that they are rather involved in probing the tissue environment and pathfinding than directly propelling the movement.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data on protrusion dynamics.

claim: Migrating HCs display a front-rear polarity with asymmetric enrichment of stable F-actin filaments at the highly contractile uropod.
source: Many amoeboid migrating cells display a front-rear polarity with asymmetric enrichment of stable F-actin filaments at the highly contractile uropod (Hind et al., 2016; Bergert et al., 2012; Lammermann and Sixt, 2009). Our finding that migrating HCs display strikingly similar polarized morphology implies that they may also use uropod contraction as a pushing force to move forward.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data on F-actin distribution and citations to previous research.

claim: HCs may use uropod contraction as a pushing force to move forward.
source: Our finding that migrating HCs display strikingly similar polarized morphology implies that they may also use uropod contraction as a pushing force to move forward.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the experimental data.

claim: The Brillouin shift maps of the INL remain relatively homogenous throughout HC migration.
source: Using in vivo Brillouin microscopy, we showed that the Brillouin shift maps of the INL remain relatively homogenous throughout HC migration.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from Brillouin microscopy.

claim: Tissue compressibility could have a permissive rather than an instructive role for HC migration.
source: That no obvious compressibility gradient was observed along the apico-basal axis of the INL during HC migration implies that tissue compressibility could have a permissive rather than an instructive role for HC migration.
evidence: This is inferred from the Brillouin microscopy data.

claim: The IPL acts as a steric hindrance through which HCs cannot penetrate in either direction.
source: This together with our finding that HCs get trapped beneath the IPL in RGC-depleted retinae strongly suggests that the IPL acts as a steric hindrance through which HCs cannot penetrate in either direction.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data in atoh7 morphants.

claim: The fibrillar arrangement of axonal and dendritic processes of the IPL poses a net-like obstacle with low porosity that is below the deformation capability threshold of HC nuclei.
source: It is plausible that the fibrillar arrangement of axonal and dendritic processes of the IPL poses a net-like obstacle with low porosity that is below the deformation capability threshold of HC nuclei, which mechanically traps HCs despite their ability to move.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the experimental data.

claim: The IPL does not act as a chemical repulsive barrier but most likely poses a structural constraint through which HCs fail to pass.
source: Hence, while we cannot exclude that chemical signals also contribute to entrapment of HCs below the IPL, our result that HCs do not reorient upon hitting the mature IPL in atoh7 morphants argues that the IPL does not act as a chemical repulsive barrier but most likely poses a structural constraint through which HCs fail to pass.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data in atoh7 morphants.

claim: The space adaptation migration mode carried out by HCs allows them to follow the 'path of least resistance' when moving in a cell-dense tissue environment in the retina.
source: Together, our data points toward the idea that the space adaptation migration mode carried out by HCs allows them to follow the 'path of least resistance' (Weber et al., 2013; Renkawitz et al., 2019; Kameritsch and Renkawitz, 2020) when moving in a cell-dense tissue environment in the retina that does not seem to provide substantial matrix components.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data and supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Multipolar migration modes are observed in many parts of the developing CNS.
source: Further, as multipolar migration modes are observed in many parts of the developing CNS, it is likely that amoeboid-like migration and behavior is widespread in diverse systems beyond the retina.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about migration in the CNS.
